subject: Copywriting
title: Watergate: Follow the Story
description: A fast breakdown of Watergate: Follow the Story for builders.

hook.text: The Washington Post's Watergate headlines brought down a president. Each one ratcheted the pressure higher.

buildup.text: The first stories were buried inside the paper. Editors didn't think a break-in mattered. They were wrong.

discovery.text: Woodward and Bernstein's headlines built a narrative over months. Each new revelation demanded a bigger headline.

twist.text: Nixon called the Post biased and tried to revoke their TV licenses. The headlines didn't stop.

climax.text: 'NIXON RESIGNS' ran on August 9, 1974. Two words that ended a presidency, driven by years of headlines.

punchline.text: Two words ended a presidency. Headlines topple power.

quiz.question: Which newspaper's headlines drove the Watergate story?

details.summary: The Washington Post's Watergate coverage, led by Woodward and Bernstein, demonstrated how persistent investigative headlines could topple a presidency. details.whyItMatters: Watergate showed that sustained headline pressure could drive political change. It established the investigative headline as a form of public accountability that persists today.
takeaways: Persistent investigative headlines built narrative pressure over months
The Post's headlines sustained public attention through a complex story
Watergate established a template for accountability journalism

faq.question: How did headlines help sustain the Watergate investigation?
faq.answer: Each headline revealed a new piece of the puzzle, building momentum. Editors crafted headlines that connected new revelations to the larger pattern of corruption. This serial narrative kept the public engaged through a story that took over two years to fully unfold.

faq.question: What did Watergate teach about headline writing?
faq.answer: It proved that factual, measured headlines could be as powerful as sensational ones. The Post resisted the temptation to editorialize and let the facts drive the headlines. This restraint built credibility that made each new revelation more devastating.
